question: Which factor can increase the risk of unintentional systemic absorption of a topical drug?

options.A: Thickened, intact stratum corneum
options.B: Compromised skin integrity such as burns or abrasions
options.C: Storing the medication in a cool, dry place
options.D: Applying the drug to the soles of the feet

explanation: Compromised skin integrity, like burns or abrasions, breaches the protective skin barrier, increasing the risk of systemic drug absorption. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h1)

question: Which layer of the skin acts as the primary physical barrier against percutaneous drug absorption?

options.A: Stratum basale
options.B: Dermis
options.C: Stratum corneum
options.D: Subcutaneous adipose layer

explanation: The stratum corneum is the outermost layer of the epidermis, forming the tough barrier that drugs must cross to be absorbed percutaneously. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h2)

question: How does skin hydration affect the percutaneous absorption of topical medications?

options.A: It significantly enhances drug penetration and absorption
options.B: It completely blocks all drug molecules from entering the skin
options.C: It deactivates the active pharmaceutical ingredients
options.D: It has no impact on absorption rates

explanation: Hydrated skin swells and loosens the barrier lipids, which significantly enhances the penetration and absorption of topical medications. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h2)

question: Which topical vehicle is oil-based, highly occlusive, and best suited for dry, thick, or scaly skin lesions?

options.A: Gel
options.B: Lotion
options.C: Ointment
options.D: Aqueous solution

explanation: Ointments are oil-based and provide high occlusiveness, trapping moisture and making them ideal for dry, thickened, or scaly skin. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h3)

question: Why are water-based gels often preferred for treating acne or application on hairy regions?

options.A: They create a heavy, greasy barrier that traps sweat
options.B: They liquefy upon skin contact and dry without leaving a greasy residue
options.C: They are highly occlusive and prevent all moisture evaporation
options.D: They contain high amounts of heavy mineral oils

explanation: Gels are water-based formulations that liquefy on contact and dry cleanly, making them ideal for acne-prone or hairy areas without feeling greasy. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h3)

question: What is the primary pharmacological action of topical corticosteroids in dermatological care?

options.A: Destruction of bacterial cell walls
options.B: Anti-inflammatory and antipruritic effects
options.C: Softening and shedding of the stratum corneum
options.D: Eradication of fungal dermatophytes

explanation: Topical corticosteroids are prescribed primarily for their powerful anti-inflammatory and antipruritic (anti-itch) properties. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h4)

question: Which adverse effect is commonly associated with the prolonged, inappropriate use of potent topical corticosteroids?

options.A: Skin atrophy and striae
options.B: Severe skin hyperpigmentation and excessive hair growth
options.C: Complete eradication of normal skin flora
options.D: Rapid thickening of the stratum corneum

explanation: Prolonged use of high-potency topical steroids thins the skin, leading to skin atrophy, striae (stretch marks), and fragility. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h4)

question: What key characteristic must all ophthalmic drops and ointments possess to prevent ocular complications?

options.A: High lipid solubility
options.B: Sterility
options.C: A heavy, greasy vehicle base
options.D: Strong systemic vasoconstrictor properties

explanation: Ophthalmic medications must be completely sterile to avoid introducing harmful pathogens that could cause serious eye infections. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h5)

question: How should a nurse correctly position the pinna when administering otic drops to an adult patient?

options.A: Downward and backward
options.B: Upward and backward
options.C: Straight outward
options.D: Forward and upward

explanation: For adults, pulling the pinna upward and backward straightens the external auditory canal, allowing ear drops to flow down properly. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h5)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to perform a baseline skin assessment prior to applying a topical medication?

options.A: To measure the patient's body mass index accurately
options.B: To evaluate therapeutic progress and monitor for adverse skin changes over time
options.C: To determine the patient's blood glucose levels
options.D: To eliminate the need for hand hygiene

explanation: Baseline skin assessments provide a reference point to evaluate treatment efficacy and detect any new adverse skin changes during follow-up. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h6)

question: What is the standard initial step in preparing a skin site for topical drug application?

options.A: Applying an occlusive plastic wrap
options.B: Scrubbing the area vigorously with an abrasive sponge
options.C: Gently cleansing the site with mild soap and water or normal saline
options.D: Applying a potent topical steroid first

explanation: Gentle cleansing with mild soap and water or normal saline removes dirt, crusts, and residual medications without irritating the skin barrier. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h6)

question: Why should nurses wear gloves when applying topical medications to a patient?

options.A: To enhance the patient's skin absorption rate
options.B: To prevent cross-contamination and unintended drug absorption through the nurse's hands
options.C: To keep the nurse's hands warm during the procedure
options.D: To replace the need for hand hygiene before the procedure

explanation: Wearing gloves protects the patient from infection and shields the nurse from absorbing potent medications through their own skin. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h7)

question: In which direction should creams or ointments generally be smoothed onto the skin?

options.A: In a vigorous circular motion against hair growth
options.B: In the direction of hair growth
options.C: Rapidly back and forth with maximum friction
options.D: Only vertically from bottom to top

explanation: Smoothing topical agents in the direction of hair growth prevents follicular irritation and painful inflammation like folliculitis. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h7)

question: What factor increases the likelihood of systemic adverse effects from topical medications?

options.A: Applying the drug to intact, thick plantar skin
options.B: Using the medication over large surface areas or broken skin
options.C: Storing the medication in a refrigerator
options.D: Using water-based lotions instead of ointments

explanation: Applying topical drugs over extensive body surfaces or compromised skin significantly increases systemic absorption and toxicity risks. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h8)

question: Which complication can arise from prolonged use of potent topical corticosteroids over large body areas?

options.A: Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression
options.B: Immediate visual acuity improvement
options.C: Rapid weight loss and dehydration
options.D: Permanent skin thickening and increased elasticity

explanation: Systemic absorption of potent topical steroids can suppress the HPA axis, leading to systemic endocrine effects. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h8)

question: What is a common reason patients fail to complete a prescribed course of topical therapy at home?

options.A: They experience immediate, permanent cure after one application
options.B: They misunderstand instructions or find the vehicles messy
options.C: Topical drugs never require hand hygiene
options.D: Physicians always provide hospitalized administration

explanation: Misunderstanding complex instructions or disliking messy vehicle formulations often leads to poor concordance in home care settings. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h9)

question: What key instruction should a nurse include when teaching a patient about applying topical medications at home?

options.A: Double-dip fingers into multi-use jars to save time
options.B: Perform hand hygiene before and after applying the medication
options.C: Apply thick layers over open wounds to speed up healing
options.D: Discontinue treatment immediately upon the slightest symptom relief without consulting the clinician

explanation: Hand hygiene before and after application prevents infection transmission and accidental transfer of medication to sensitive areas like the eyes. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h9)

question: Which primary host cell receptor is targeted by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)?

options.A: CD8 receptors
options.B: CD4 receptors
options.C: Beta receptors
options.D: Alpha receptors

explanation: HIV primarily targets and infects cells bearing CD4 receptors, such as helper T-lymphocytes, monocytes, and macrophages. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h1)

question: What is the primary goal of Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) in managing HIV?

options.A: To completely eradicate the virus from the body
options.B: To convert double-stranded RNA into single-stranded DNA
options.C: To suppress viral replication to undetectable levels and preserve immune function
options.D: To stimulate the rapid destruction of CD4+ T-cells

explanation: ART suppresses viral replication to undetectable levels, which halts CD4+ T-cell destruction and allows the immune system to recover. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h1)

question: How do Nucleoside and Nucleotide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) primarily function?

options.A: By blocking viral entry into the host cell
options.B: By acting as decoy substrates that terminate the viral DNA chain
options.C: By inhibiting the viral protease enzyme cleavage process
options.D: By directly integrating into the host cell's chromosome

explanation: NRTIs act as decoy substrates that cause premature termination of the viral DNA chain synthesized by reverse transcriptase. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h2)

question: What is the specific mechanism of action of Protease Inhibitors (PIs)?

options.A: They prevent the viral protease from cleaving polyproteins into mature functional units
options.B: They bind directly to the reverse transcriptase enzyme to alter its conformation
options.C: They prevent the viral DNA from entering the nucleus of the host cell
options.D: They block CD4 receptors on helper T-lymphocytes

explanation: PIs inhibit the viral protease enzyme, preventing it from cleaving polyproteins into mature, infectious virions. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h2)

question: What is the preferred first-line ART backbone combination in Nigeria for treatment-naive adults?

options.A: Zidovudine plus Nevirapine
options.B: Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate plus Lamivudine or Emtricitabine
options.C: Abacavir plus Efavirenz
options.D: Lopinavir plus Ritonavir

explanation: Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF) combined with Lamivudine (3TC) or Emtricitabine (FTC) forms the preferred NRTI backbone for first-line regimens in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h3)

question: When is a second-line antiretroviral regimen typically initiated in a patient?

options.A: Immediately upon the initial diagnosis of HIV
options.B: When the patient reports minor gastrointestinal side effects
options.C: When there is confirmed treatment failure and persistent viral load rebound
options.D: After the patient successfully completes six months of first-line therapy

explanation: Second-line regimens are deployed when a patient experiences confirmed treatment failure indicated by persistent viral load rebound. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h3)

question: What level of patient adherence is typically required for successful long-term antiretroviral therapy?

options.A: At least 50% of prescribed doses
options.B: At least 75% of prescribed doses
options.C: At least 95% of prescribed doses
options.D: 100% adherence without any missing doses ever

explanation: Strict patient adherence of at least 95% of prescribed doses on time is essential to maintain viral suppression and prevent resistance. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h4)

question: What is the primary consequence of poor or suboptimal patient adherence to antiretroviral therapy?

options.A: Immediate hepatic failure
options.B: Development of drug-resistant viral strains and viral rebound
options.C: Enhanced absorption of the medication
options.D: Permanent cure of the HIV infection

explanation: Poor adherence leads to viral rebound and is the primary driver behind the development of drug-resistant viral strains. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h4)

question: Which organ system is primarily monitored for long-term toxicity when a patient is prescribed Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate?

options.A: The renal system
options.B: The pulmonary system
options.C: The cardiovascular system
options.D: The integumentary system

explanation: Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate is associated with renal impairment and bone mineral density loss, making kidney function monitoring essential. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h5)

question: What is a major hypersensitivity screening consideration before initiating Abacavir therapy?

options.A: Testing for the HLA-B*5701 allele
options.B: Checking fasting blood glucose levels
options.C: Performing a baseline CD4 cell count
options.D: Measuring liver transaminases

explanation: Baseline genetic testing for the HLA-B*5701 allele is recommended before starting Abacavir to prevent severe hypersensitivity reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h5)

question: Which enzyme system is primarily responsible for the pharmacokinetic interactions seen with many antiretroviral drugs?

options.A: Hepatic cytochrome P450 enzyme system
options.B: Renal tubular secretion system
options.C: Gastric acid secretory pathways
options.D: Pancreatic amylase enzyme system

explanation: Many antiretrovirals interact with hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, leading to significant potential for drug-drug interactions. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h6)

question: What is the primary cause of drug resistance in patients taking antiretroviral therapy?

options.A: Consuming a high-fat diet with every meal
options.B: Viral replication occurring in the presence of suboptimal drug levels
options.C: Taking too many medications from different classes simultaneously
options.D: Natural genetic immunity of the host cell

explanation: Drug resistance emerges when mutations occur during ongoing viral replication while drug levels are suboptimal due to poor adherence or interactions. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h6)

question: Why is achieving rapid viral suppression vital for pregnant women living with HIV?

options.A: To prevent mother-to-child transmission of the virus
options.B: To completely eliminate the need for infant prophylaxis
options.C: To prevent gestational diabetes mellitus
options.D: To avoid the need for hepatic function testing

explanation: Rapid and sustained viral suppression in pregnant women is essential to prevent mother-to-child transmission during gestation, labor, and breastfeeding. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h7)

question: What is a major management consideration when treating an HIV-infected patient who has a co-infection with Tuberculosis?

options.A: Rifampicin acts as an enzyme inducer that can significantly lower antiretroviral drug concentrations
options.B: Anti-TB drugs completely eliminate the need for antiretroviral therapy
options.C: Pediatric liquid formulations must be used for all adult co-infected patients
options.D: Viral load monitoring is completely unnecessary during TB treatment

explanation: Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer that lowers antiretroviral concentrations, requiring careful regimen adjustments and timing. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h7)

question: What is a key nursing responsibility when educating a patient newly initiated on antiretroviral therapy?

options.A: Emphasizing the critical importance of lifelong adherence to the treatment regimen
options.B: Instructing the patient to stop taking medications once viral load becomes undetectable
options.C: Ensuring the patient diagnoses their own drug resistance mutations
options.D: Prescribing alternative second-line regimens independently

explanation: Nurses must educate patients thoroughly on the critical importance of lifelong adherence to maintain viral suppression and health. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h8)

question: How can nurses best help patients manage minor adverse effects like nausea caused by their medications?

options.A: Advise the patient to abruptly discontinue all treatment
options.B: Provide practical guidance such as taking specific medications with food
options.C: Recommend doubling the next dose to build tolerance
options.D: Instruct the patient to avoid reporting symptoms to the clinic

explanation: Nurses provide practical advice, such as taking certain medications with food, to help patients manage minor gastrointestinal side effects. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h8)

question: What is the primary pharmacological action of anticoagulants?

options.A: To actively dissolve already formed blood clots
options.B: To disrupt the coagulation cascade and prevent new clot formation
options.C: To stimulate platelet aggregation and primary hemostasis
options.D: To increase the concentration of circulating fibrinogen

explanation: Anticoagulants work by slowing down the clotting process and disrupting the coagulation cascade, which prevents new clots from forming or existing ones from growing, unlike thrombolytics which dissolve clots. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h1)

question: Which phase of hemostasis involves the conversion of soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin strands?

options.A: Primary hemostasis
options.B: Secondary hemostasis
options.C: Vasoconstriction phase
options.D: Fibrinolysis phase

explanation: Secondary hemostasis involves the activation of the coagulation cascade, which ultimately converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin to stabilize the platelet plug. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h1)

question: How do indirect anticoagulants like heparins primarily exert their anticoagulant effect?

options.A: By directly binding to and neutralizing Factor Xa without any cofactors
options.B: By inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase in the liver
options.C: By potentiating antithrombin III to neutralize clotting factors like thrombin and Factor Xa
options.D: By directly dissolving existing fibrin strands in the blood vessel

explanation: Heparins act indirectly by binding to and potentiating antithrombin III, which then rapidly inactivates clotting factors such as thrombin (Factor IIa) and Factor Xa. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h2)

question: Which of the following describes the mechanism of action of vitamin K antagonists like warfarin?

options.A: Potentiation of antithrombin III activity
options.B: Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing activation of specific clotting factors
options.C: Direct and selective inhibition of free thrombin
options.D: Direct stimulation of fibrinolytic pathways

explanation: Warfarin works by inhibiting the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, which prevents the activation of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X in the liver. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h2)

question: Which laboratory test is routinely used to monitor the therapeutic effect of unfractionated heparin (UFH)?

options.A: Prothrombin Time (PT)
options.B: Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT)
options.C: International Normalized Ratio (INR)
options.D: Complete Blood Count (platelets only)

explanation: Unfractionated heparin therapy is routinely monitored using the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) to ensure the patient is within the therapeutic range. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h3)

question: What is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)?

options.A: An allergic skin rash caused by subcutaneous LMWH injections
options.B: An immune-mediated reaction causing a drop in platelets and high thrombosis risk
options.C: A genetic condition causing resistance to heparin therapy
options.D: A permanent destruction of red blood cells caused by high-dose UFH

explanation: HIT is an immune-mediated adverse reaction to heparin characterized by a paradoxical drop in platelet counts alongside a significantly increased risk of developing dangerous blood clots. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h3)

question: What standardized laboratory measure is used to monitor a patient taking warfarin?

options.A: Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT)
options.B: International Normalized Ratio (INR)
options.C: Bleeding time
options.D: Platelet aggregation assay

explanation: The International Normalized Ratio (INR) is the standardized laboratory measure used globally to monitor and adjust warfarin therapy safety. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h4)

question: Why must patients on warfarin maintain consistent dietary intake of vitamin K?

options.A: Vitamin K increases the risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
options.B: Fluctuations in vitamin K can drastically alter the anticoagulant effect and INR levels
options.C: Vitamin K serves as the primary reversal agent to be taken daily with the medication
options.D: Vitamin K deficiency causes immediate destruction of mechanical heart valves

explanation: Since warfarin works by antagonizing vitamin K, sudden changes in dietary vitamin K intake can destabilize the patient's anticoagulation level and make INR control difficult. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h4)

question: Which of the following drugs is classified as a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) that inhibits Factor Xa?

options.A: Warfarin
options.B: Unfractionated Heparin
options.C: Apixaban
options.D: Dabigatran

explanation: Apixaban is a direct oral anticoagulant that specifically targets and inhibits Factor Xa, whereas dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h5)

question: What is a major advantage of DOACs compared to traditional vitamin K antagonists like warfarin?

options.A: They require lifelong daily intravenous administration
options.B: They do not require routine coagulation monitoring like INR checks and have fewer food interactions
options.C: They have an infinite half-life making missed doses completely inconsequential
options.D: They are completely independent of renal function for elimination

explanation: DOACs offer predictable pharmacokinetics, fewer food interactions, and eliminate the need for routine INR monitoring, which simplifies long-term therapy. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h5)

question: Why are anticoagulants prescribed for patients with atrial fibrillation?

options.A: To normalize the electrical heart rhythm and eliminate ectopic pacemakers
options.B: To prevent cardioembolic stroke caused by blood stasis and clot formation in the atria
options.C: To actively dissolve atherosclerotic plaques in the coronary arteries
options.D: To permanently lower systemic blood pressure in hypertensive crisis

explanation: Atrial fibrillation causes irregular contractions and blood stasis in the heart chambers, increasing clot formation risk; anticoagulants prevent these clots from traveling to the brain as a stroke. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h6)

question: Which of the following is a common postoperative indication for prophylactic anticoagulants?

options.A: Total knee or hip replacement surgery
options.B: Routine uncomplicated appendectomy
options.C: Superficial skin laceration repair
options.D: Cataract extraction surgery

explanation: Orthopedic surgeries like total hip or knee replacements significantly increase the risk of venous thromboembolism, making postoperative prophylactic anticoagulation essential. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h6)

question: What is the specific pharmacological reversal agent for unfractionated heparin?

options.A: Vitamin K
options.B: Protamine sulfate
options.C: Idarucizumab
options.D: Fresh frozen plasma

explanation: Protamine sulfate is the specific antidote that binds to and neutralizes unfractionated heparin, rapidly reversing its anticoagulant effects. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h7)

question: Which reversal agent is specifically used to neutralize the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran?

options.A: Andexanet alfa
options.B: Protamine sulfate
options.C: Idarucizumab
options.D: Vitamin K

explanation: Idarucizumab is a specific monoclonal antibody fragment approved to rapidly reverse the anticoagulant effect of dabigatran in emergency situations. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h7)

question: What lifestyle or hygiene adjustment should a nurse recommend to a patient on anticoagulant therapy?

options.A: Use stiff-bristled toothbrushes to thoroughly clean the gums
options.B: Use an electric razor instead of a traditional blade to prevent skin cuts
options.C: Engage in high-contact sports to maintain cardiovascular fitness
options.D: Stop all physical exercise immediately and remain on strict bed rest

explanation: Using an electric razor minimizes the risk of accidental skin nicks and cuts, which can lead to prolonged bleeding in patients taking anticoagulants. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h8)

question: Which of the following symptoms reported by a patient on anticoagulation therapy requires immediate medical attention?

options.A: Mild fatigue after normal daily activities
options.B: Dark, tarry stools (melena) or blood in the urine
options.C: Transient mild bruising on the forearm after minor bumping
options.D: Slight metallic taste in the mouth

explanation: Dark, tarry stools (melena) and hematuria are signs of gastrointestinal or urinary tract bleeding, which are serious adverse events requiring immediate intervention. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T14#GNS215_U6_T14_h8)

question: What is the primary physiological purpose of haemostasis in the human body?

options.A: To accelerate heart rate during stress
options.B: To halt bleeding following vascular injury
options.C: To stimulate red blood cell production
options.D: To increase blood pressure rapidly

explanation: Haemostasis is the critical physiological process the body employs to stop bleeding after a blood vessel is injured. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h1)

question: Which of the following describes the role of secondary haemostasis?

options.A: Initial vasoconstriction of the blood vessel
options.B: Dissolving the blood clot after healing
options.C: Involving the coagulation cascade to form a stable fibrin mesh
options.D: Releasing histamine to dilate capillaries

explanation: Secondary haemostasis involves the activation of the coagulation cascade, resulting in the formation of a stable fibrin mesh that reinforces the initial platelet plug. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h1)

question: How do antifibrinolytic agents like tranexamic acid primarily work?

options.A: By destroying platelets
options.B: By preventing the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin
options.C: By directly replacing Vitamin K in the liver
options.D: By causing immediate systemic vasoconstriction

explanation: Antifibrinolytic agents block lysine binding sites on plasminogen, which prevents its conversion to plasmin and stops the breakdown of fibrin clots. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h2)

question: What is the primary difference between systemic and topical antihaemorrhagic agents?

options.A: Topical agents circulate throughout the whole body.
options.B: Systemic agents are only used for skin cuts.
options.C: Topical agents are applied directly to a bleeding site, whereas systemic agents circulate in the body.
options.D: Systemic agents require no liver metabolism.

explanation: Topical agents act locally at the wound surface, while systemic agents circulate through the bloodstream to affect the entire coagulation system. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h2)

question: Which systemic agent is commonly used to reverse the effects of warfarin or treat hemorrhagic disease of the newborn?

options.A: Tranexamic acid
options.B: Vitamin K
options.C: Protamine sulfate
options.D: Desmopressin

explanation: Vitamin K acts as an essential cofactor for hepatic synthesis of several clotting factors and is used to reverse warfarin and treat newborn bleeding disorders. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h3)

question: Why is careful monitoring of laboratory values such as PT, INR, and aPTT essential when administering systemic haemostatic agents?

options.A: To measure the patient's blood glucose levels
options.B: To assess kidney function before drug excretion
options.C: To evaluate the patient's baseline clotting status and prevent thrombotic complications
options.D: To determine the exact blood type of the patient

explanation: Systemic agents affect total body coagulation, so tracking clotting times helps ensure safe dosing and prevents excessive clotting or thrombosis. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h3)

question: How do gelatin sponges and oxidized regenerated cellulose primarily achieve local haemostasis?

options.A: By systemic liver stimulation
options.B: By providing a physical matrix that absorbs blood and encourages platelet aggregation
options.C: By dissolving existing fibrin clots completely
options.D: By causing systemic vasodilation

explanation: These agents act mechanically by absorbing blood, swelling, and forming a structural framework that promotes rapid platelet clumping at the wound site. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h4)

question: What is the direct action of topical thrombin when applied to a wound?

options.A: It destroys red blood cells.
options.B: It dilates local blood vessels to flush out debris.
options.C: It directly converts fibrinogen into fibrin to form a solid clot.
options.D: It inhibits platelet adhesion.

explanation: Topical thrombin directly catalyses the conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin, rapidly generating a solid clot at the specific site of application. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h4)

question: In which clinical scenario are agents like tranexamic acid and oxytocin frequently deployed in obstetrics?

options.A: Induction of labor in post-term pregnancies
options.B: Management and prevention of severe postpartum hemorrhage
options.C: Treatment of gestational diabetes mellitus
options.D: Prevention of pregnancy-induced hypertension

explanation: These agents are frontline defenses used to manage and prevent severe postpartum hemorrhage caused by uterine atony or surgical tearing. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h5)

question: Why might patients with von Willebrand disease receive desmopressin prior to an invasive procedure?

options.A: To lower their blood pressure during surgery
options.B: To stimulate the release of stored von Willebrand factor and factor VIII to prevent excessive bleeding
options.C: To act as a general anesthetic agent
options.D: To prevent postoperative wound infections

explanation: Desmopressin helps release stored von Willebrand factor and factor VIII, bolstering the clotting capacity of patients with von Willebrand disease before invasive procedures. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h5)

question: What is a primary contraindication for the administration of most systemic antihaemorrhagic and antifibrinolytic agents?

options.A: Active thromboembolic disease such as a pulmonary embolism
options.B: Mild iron deficiency anemia
options.C: History of seasonal allergic rhinitis
options.D: Low-grade fever following surgery

explanation: Giving procoagulant or antifibrinolytic agents to a patient with active thromboembolic disease can worsen clot formation and cause vessel blockage. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h6)

question: Why is it important for nurses to check patient allergy histories before applying animal-derived topical agents like bovine thrombin?

options.A: To prevent dietary restrictions after surgery
options.B: To avoid severe hypersensitivity or allergic reactions
options.C: To ensure the drug is compatible with intravenous fluids
options.D: To check if the patient is allergic to latex gloves

explanation: Animal-derived agents can trigger severe hypersensitivity or allergic reactions if the patient is sensitive to those specific biological proteins. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h6)

question: What is the most significant systemic risk associated with the overuse or inappropriate administration of antihaemorrhagic agents?

options.A: Severe hypoglycemia
options.B: Unwanted thrombotic events such as deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
options.C: Chronic hypertension
options.D: Permanent kidney failure requiring dialysis

explanation: Because these drugs promote clotting, excessive or inappropriate administration can push the body into a hypercoagulable state, causing dangerous blood clots. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h7)

question: Which nursing assessment finding could indicate a potential deep vein thrombosis as a complication of haemostatic therapy?

options.A: Unilateral calf swelling and tenderness
options.B: Generalized skin rash on the trunk
options.C: Elevated blood glucose levels
options.D: Decreased bowel sounds

explanation: Unilateral calf swelling, pain, and tenderness are classic clinical signs of a deep vein thrombosis developing in the lower extremities. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h7)

question: What is a primary nursing responsibility prior to administering a systemic antihaemorrhagic agent?

options.A: Discharging the patient immediately
options.B: Verifying baseline coagulation profiles, renal function, and allergy history
options.C: Performing a complete neurological examination every 5 minutes
options.D: Administering a high-fat meal to enhance absorption

explanation: Before giving these drugs, nurses must check baseline labs, organ function, and allergies to ensure safety and prevent adverse reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h8)

question: How does a nurse evaluate the successful therapeutic efficacy of an antihaemorrhagic agent following administration?

options.A: By observing a decrease in blood loss and stabilization of vital signs
options.B: By noting an increase in body temperature
options.C: By confirming the patient's favorite food
options.D: By recording an increase in daily fluid intake

explanation: The ultimate goal of antihaemorrhagic therapy is to stop bleeding, which is evaluated by reduced blood loss and stable vital signs. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T15#GNS215_U6_T15_h8)

question: Which cells in the human body are primarily responsible for producing antibodies against foreign antigens?

options.A: Red blood cells
options.B: B-lymphocytes
options.C: Platelets
options.D: Epithelial cells

explanation: B-lymphocytes are specialized white blood cells that produce targeted proteins called antibodies to neutralize foreign pathogens. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h1)

question: What is the primary purpose of introducing a weakened or killed pathogen into the body via a vaccine?

options.A: To cause a severe clinical infection
options.B: To permanently weaken the immune system
options.C: To stimulate immunological memory without causing the actual disease
options.D: To replace the need for white blood cells

explanation: Vaccines introduce harmless variants or pieces of pathogens to safely stimulate a primary immune response and build immunological memory. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h1)

question: Why must live-attenuated vaccines be administered with extreme caution to immunocompromised patients?

options.A: They are completely ineffective in all populations
options.B: The weakened pathogen could potentially cause severe disease due to uncontrolled replication
options.C: They instantly destroy all existing antibodies in the blood
options.D: They contain live bacterial toxins that require immediate antitoxin administration

explanation: Live-attenuated vaccines contain active, weakened organisms that can replicate and potentially cause severe infection in individuals with compromised immune systems. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h2)

question: What type of vaccine uses specific pieces of a germ, such as proteins or sugars, rather than the whole organism?

options.A: Live-attenuated vaccine
options.B: Toxoid vaccine
options.C: Subunit, recombinant, or conjugate vaccine
options.D: Whole-cell inactivated vaccine

explanation: Subunit, recombinant, polysaccharide, and conjugate vaccines utilize specific fragments or pieces of the pathogen to stimulate a focused immune response. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h2)

question: Which cells are responsible for presenting processed vaccine antigens to naive T-helper cells in the lymph nodes?

options.A: Red blood cells
options.B: Antigen-presenting cells like dendritic cells
options.C: Platelets
options.D: Endothelial cells

explanation: Antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells capture vaccine components, process them, and present them to T-helper cells to initiate the adaptive response. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h3)

question: What is the primary benefit of memory cells created during vaccination?

options.A: They slow down the immune response to prevent inflammation
options.B: They destroy all normal flora in the gastrointestinal tract
options.C: They recognize future exposures to the pathogen and mount a rapid, magnified secondary response
options.D: They produce red blood cells to combat anemia caused by infection

explanation: Memory cells persist long-term to provide a swift and powerful defense if the body encounters the actual pathogen later in life. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h3)

question: Which vaccines are typically administered to a newborn baby immediately at birth in Nigeria?

options.A: Measles and Yellow Fever
options.B: BCG, Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV 0), and Hepatitis B
options.C: MMR and Varicella
options.D: Tetanus toxoid and Meningococcal conjugate

explanation: At birth, infants in Nigeria receive BCG for tuberculosis, OPV zero dose for polio, and the birth dose of Hepatitis B. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h4)

question: Around what age are measles and yellow fever vaccines typically scheduled for administration under the Nigerian immunization program?

options.A: At birth
options.B: At 6 weeks of age
options.C: At 9 months of age
options.D: At 5 years of age

explanation: Measles and yellow fever vaccines are generally scheduled around 9 months of age to ensure optimal seroconversion and protection. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h4)

question: What is the standard recommended storage temperature range for most refrigerated vaccines in a clinic setting?

options.B: +2°C to +8°C

explanation: Refrigerated vaccines must be kept between +2°C and +8°C to maintain their potency and prevent thermal degradation. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h5)

question: Which injection route and anatomical site are standard for administering the pentavalent vaccine to an infant?

options.A: Intradermal on the left forearm
options.B: Subcutaneous on the upper arm
options.C: Intramuscular in the anterolateral thigh
options.D: Intravenous in the dorsal hand vein

explanation: Pentavalent vaccine is administered via the intramuscular route into the anterolateral aspect of the infant's thigh. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h5)

question: How long is it generally recommended to observe a patient in the clinic after vaccine administration to monitor for immediate adverse reactions?

options.A: 1 to 2 minutes
options.B: 15 to 30 minutes
options.C: 2 to 3 hours
options.D: 24 hours

explanation: Patients should be observed for 15 to 30 minutes post-vaccination to quickly identify and treat immediate severe hypersensitivity reactions like anaphylaxis. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h6)

question: Which agency in Nigeria is primarily responsible for receiving and monitoring reports of Adverse Events Following Immunization (AEFI)?

options.A: NAFDAC
options.B: Nigerian Police Force
options.C: Federal Ministry of Education
options.D: Standard Organization of Nigeria

explanation: NAFDAC (National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control) handles drug and vaccine pharmacovigilance and safety reporting in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h6)

question: What is the appropriate nursing action when a child presents with a moderate to severe acute illness and high fever on the scheduled vaccination day?

options.A: Administer all scheduled vaccines immediately regardless of fever
options.B: Permanently ban the child from ever receiving vaccines
options.C: Defer vaccination as a precaution until the acute illness has resolved
options.D: Double the dose of live vaccines to fight the current illness

explanation: Moderate or severe acute illness serves as a precaution, prompting nurses to defer vaccination until recovery to avoid confusing symptoms or impairing immune response. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h7)

question: Which type of vaccine is generally contraindicated for pregnant women and severely immunocompromised individuals?

options.A: Inactivated vaccines
options.B: Live-attenuated vaccines
options.C: Toxoid vaccines
options.D: Subunit conjugate vaccines

explanation: Live-attenuated vaccines contain active, replicating organisms and are typically contraindicated during pregnancy and severe immunosuppression due to safety risks. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h7)

question: How is vaccine hesitancy best defined in a public health context?

options.A: A complete lack of vaccines in hospital pharmacies
options.B: The reluctance or refusal to vaccinate despite the availability of vaccination services
options.C: An allergic reaction occurring immediately after an injection
options.D: The failure to maintain proper cold chain temperatures

explanation: Vaccine hesitancy refers to delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite availability, requiring targeted nursing education and advocacy. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h8)

question: What is an effective strategy for nurses to address community rumors and myths regarding immunization?

options.A: Scaring patients with graphic descriptions of diseases
options.B: Ignoring community questions and enforcing mandatory rules without explanation
options.C: Using empathetic, culturally sensitive, and evidence-based communication
options.D: Halting all vaccination clinics until community members ask for them

explanation: Empathetic, culturally appropriate communication and education help build trust and dispel myths regarding vaccines. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h8)

question: What does the Pearl Index measure when evaluating family planning methods?

options.A: The cost-effectiveness ratio of public health contraceptive distribution
options.B: The average duration of pharmacological effectiveness for a single dose
options.C: The number of unintended pregnancies per 100 women-years of exposure
options.D: The percentage of users who experience severe metabolic side effects

explanation: The Pearl Index is the standard epidemiological metric used to calculate the failure rate of birth control methods in clinical trials. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h1)

question: Why is there typically a significant difference between perfect use and typical use failure rates for oral medications?

options.A: Metabolic enzymes in the liver degrade active chemical compounds faster over time
options.B: Manufacturers intentionally underreport laboratory efficacy to avoid liability issues
options.C: Human behavioral factors and inconsistent daily adherence affect real-world outcomes
options.D: Generic drug formulations have lower bioavailability than brand-name alternatives

explanation: While a drug may work perfectly when taken at the exact same hour every day, everyday human error introduces missed doses that raise the real-world pregnancy rate. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h1)

question: Which hormonal surge is directly suppressed by exogenous estrogen and progestin to prevent ovulation?

options.A: Thyroid stimulating hormone
options.B: Luteinizing hormone
options.C: Adrenocorticotropic hormone
options.D: Growth hormone

explanation: The mid-cycle surge of luteinizing hormone triggers the release of an egg from the ovary, which hormonal contraceptives successfully block via negative feedback. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h2)

question: How do progestin components primarily prevent fertilization at the level of the cervix?

options.A: By thickening cervical secretions to create a physical barrier against sperm transit
options.B: By increasing vaginal pH to actively immobilize sperm cells upon contact
options.C: By stimulating ciliated epithelial cells to sweep sperm backward out of the os
options.D: By releasing spermicidal enzymes directly into the endocervical glands

explanation: Progestins alter the consistency of cervical mucus so that spermatozoa cannot easily swim through the cervical canal to reach the uterine cavity. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h2)

question: What is the standard dosing frequency for depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injections?

options.A: Every four weeks
options.B: Every six months
options.C: Once a year
options.D: Every three months

explanation: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is a long-acting injectable progestin administered intramuscularly or subcutaneously every 12 to 13 weeks. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h3)

question: A client using a 28-day combined oral contraceptive pack inquires about the purpose of the final seven pills that contain no hormones. What is the best clinical response?

options.A: They supply essential dietary iron and vitamins lost during menstruation
options.B: They maintain daily pill-taking habits and trigger a scheduled withdrawal bleed
options.C: They serve as active backup protection during the mid-cycle ovulation phase
options.D: They prevent sudden hormonal withdrawal headaches and severe mood swings

explanation: The inactive pills keep the user in a continuous daily routine so they do not lose track of when to start the next active blister pack, while hormone drop-off causes the bleeding. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h3)

question: Why must progestin-only oral pills be taken within a very strict daily time window?

options.A: Missing an hour causes immediate shedding of the entire endometrial lining
options.B: Strict timing prevents severe gastrointestinal distress and nausea
options.C: Hepatic enzymes break down the synthetic molecule within sixty minutes
options.D: They have a short half-life and rely on rapid clearance of cervical changes

explanation: Because mini-pills contain low doses of hormone and no estrogen, their protective cervical mucus effects wane rapidly if a dose is delayed by more than a few hours. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h4)

question: How do emergency contraceptive pills primarily prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse?

options.A: By inducing immediate sloughing of the endometrium to stop implantation
options.B: By creating a toxic chemical environment that neutralizes active sperm
options.C: By destroying fertilized embryos currently traveling down the fallopian tube
options.D: By delaying or inhibiting the release of an oocyte from the ovary

explanation: Emergency contraception works by pushing back ovulation so that sperm introduced during intercourse die off before an egg becomes available for fertilization. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h4)

question: Which contraceptive category offers the unique dual benefit of preventing both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections?

options.A: Subdermal implants
options.B: Combined oral pills
options.C: Barrier methods
options.D: Progestin injectables

explanation: Condoms and other physical barriers physically block the exchange of bodily fluids, protecting against infections while stopping sperm transit. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h5)

question: What is the primary mechanism by which copper intrauterine devices prevent conception?

options.A: Secreting high levels of synthetic estrogen to block pituitary hormones
options.B: Inducing permanent blockage of the proximal fallopian tubes via scarring
options.C: Releasing copper ions that impair sperm motility and viability
options.D: Absorbing all cervical secretions to prevent any sperm from entering

explanation: The local presence of copper creates an inflammatory reaction toxic to spermatozoa, inhibiting their movement and fertilizing capacity. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h5)

question: What does the letter 'C' stand for in the ACHES acronym used to monitor dangerous side effects of combined hormonal contraceptives?

options.A: Chest pain
options.B: Cramping pain
options.C: Cervical cancer
options.D: Chronic cough

explanation: Chest pain is a critical warning sign of pulmonary embolism or myocardial infarction, which are serious thromboembolic complications associated with estrogen. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h6)

question: A client on a combined oral contraceptive reports mild breast tenderness and bloating. Which hormonal component or imbalance is most directly responsible for these symptoms?

options.A: Estrogen excess
options.B: Complete progesterone block
options.C: Androgen withdrawal
options.D: Progestin deficiency

explanation: Excess estrogen levels commonly promote fluid retention and localized tissue sensitivity, resulting in breast tenderness and mild abdominal bloating. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h6)

question: Which patient demographic faces a severely heightened cardiovascular risk when using combined hormonal contraceptives containing estrogen?

options.A: Smokers over the age of 35 years
options.B: Clients with a history of mild gestational diabetes
options.C: Women diagnosed with iron-deficiency anemia
options.D: Adolescents experiencing irregular menstrual cycles

explanation: The synergistic effect of smoking and exogenous estrogen drastically increases the incidence of fatal cardiovascular events and stroke in older reproductive-age women. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h7)

question: A client with tuberculosis is prescribed rifampicin alongside her routine combined oral contraceptive pills. What is the most crucial clinical instruction to provide?

options.A: Take the oral contraceptive at night to avoid direct chemical interference in the stomach
options.B: Use a reliable non-hormonal backup method because enzyme induction lowers contraceptive efficacy
options.C: Double the daily dose of the contraceptive pill to compensate for rapid renal excretion
options.D: Switch immediately to a progestin-only injectable to bypass first-pass liver metabolism

explanation: Rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes that metabolize contraceptive hormones too quickly, rendering the pills ineffective and demanding a barrier backup. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h7)

question: Why is cultural and social assessment a critical component of family planning nursing care in Nigeria?

options.A: Nutritional deficiencies in the region completely prevent hormonal absorption in the gut
options.B: Traditional herbal remedies interfere with all modern synthetic hormone structures
options.C: Local myths, partner dynamics, and community stigma can heavily influence compliance and method choice
options.D: Government policy mandates that husbands must sign all pharmaceutical prescription forms

explanation: Addressing cultural misconceptions and involving partners supportively helps ensure adherence and reduces the abandonment of effective contraceptive methods. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h8)

question: A young female client expresses fear that taking a progestin implant will cause permanent sterility after removal. What is the appropriate nursing intervention?

options.A: Instruct her to double her vitamin intake to protect her reproductive organs from damage
options.B: Confirm her fears and suggest she wait until after marriage to start any contraception
options.C: Provide empathetic education explaining that fertility typically returns promptly after discontinuation
options.D: Advise her to avoid hormonal methods entirely and rely solely on calendar calculation

explanation: Dispelling common myths with clear, reassuring facts helps alleviate client anxiety and promotes informed, autonomous reproductive healthcare decisions. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T17#GNS215_U6_T17_h8)

question: What is the primary objective of Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT)?

options.A: To provide total parenteral nutrition
options.B: To prevent or correct fluid and electrolyte deficits from dehydration
options.C: To cure bacterial infections causing gastroenteritis
options.D: To stimulate immediate peristalsis in the large intestine

explanation: ORT aims to safely restore lost fluids and electrolytes in patients suffering from dehydration due to conditions like diarrhea and vomiting. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h1)

question: Which of the following is an early clinical sign of dehydration that nursing students should assess?

options.A: Hypertension
options.B: Decreased skin turgor and dry mucous membranes
options.C: Bounding peripheral pulses
options.D: Flushed, moist skin

explanation: Dry mucous membranes and decreased skin turgor are classic signs indicating that the body is lacking adequate fluid volume. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h1)

question: Which transporter protein in the small intestine is responsible for the coupled uptake of sodium and glucose during ORT?

options.A: Sodium-potassium ATPase pump
options.B: Sodium-glucose linked transporter 1 (SGLT1)
options.C: Calcium channel blocker
options.D: Hydrogen potassium ATPase

explanation: SGLT1 is the specific brush border cotransporter that moves sodium and glucose together into the enterocyte, facilitating water absorption. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h2)

question: Why does ORS remain effective even during severe secretory diarrhea caused by pathogens like cholera?

options.A: Pathogens destroy the intestinal lining entirely
options.B: The SGLT1 transport mechanism remains functional despite toxin action
options.C: Glucose blocks the production of cholera toxin
options.D: Sodium is absorbed independently of any water movement

explanation: Even when other secretory pathways are compromised by infection, the sodium-glucose cotransporter mechanism remains intact to pull water into the body. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h2)

question: What is the primary clinical advantage of the updated low-osmolarity ORS formulation over older, higher-osmolarity preparations?

options.A: It increases stool output and speeds up transit time
options.B: It decreases stool output, reduces vomiting, and lowers the need for IV fluids
options.C: It tastes sweet enough to require no water dilution
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for potassium supplementation

explanation: Low-osmolarity ORS is proven to reduce stool volume, lessen vomiting, and minimize the necessity for intravenous fluid therapy. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h3)

question: What is the clinical role of trisodium citrate dihydrate included in the standard WHO ORS formula?

options.A: To sweeten the solution for pediatric acceptance
options.B: To act as a buffer correcting metabolic acidosis
options.C: To stimulate aggressive bowel movements
options.D: To preserve the powder shelf-life indefinitely

explanation: Citrate acts as a buffering agent that helps correct metabolic acidosis commonly seen in patients with severe dehydration from diarrhea. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h3)

question: Where does the primary absorption and mechanism of action of ORS take place?

options.A: In the stomach lining via direct gastric mucosa uptake
options.B: In the small intestine via the SGLT1 pathway
options.C: In the renal tubules of the kidneys
options.D: In the large intestine through bacterial fermentation

explanation: ORS acts primarily in the small intestine, utilizing the SGLT1 cotransporter to move sodium, glucose, and water into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h4)

question: How does ORS affect the course of an infectious diarrheal illness?

options.A: It destroys the pathogen causing the infection
options.B: It immediately paralyzes the bowels to stop diarrhea
options.C: It maintains hydration and electrolyte balance while the body fights the infection
options.D: It acts as a potent broad-spectrum antibiotic

explanation: ORS does not cure the infection itself; its role is to keep the patient hydrated and stable while the illness runs its course or is treated. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h4)

question: Which of the following clinical signs is indicative of 'Some Dehydration' according to WHO guidelines?

options.A: Coma and unresponsiveness
options.B: Restlessness, irritability, and sunken eyes
options.C: Hypertension and flushed skin
options.D: Rapidly bouncing peripheral pulses

explanation: Restlessness, irritability, and sunken eyes are classic indicators of moderate or 'some' dehydration requiring supervised ORT. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h5)

question: What skin pinch finding points toward 'Severe Dehydration'?

options.A: Skin pinch snaps back immediately in under one second
options.B: Skin pinch remains elevated or goes back very slowly (longer than two seconds)
options.C: Skin pinch is impossible to perform due to edema
options.D: Skin pinch turns red and warm

explanation: A very slow skin recoil (longer than two seconds) is a hallmark clinical sign of severe fluid deficit and poor skin turgor. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h5)

question: Within what timeframe must a prepared batch of WHO ORS solution be consumed or discarded?

options.A: 6 hours
options.B: 12 hours
options.C: 24 hours
options.D: 72 hours

explanation: Prepared ORS must be used within 24 hours to prevent microbial growth and contamination in the solution. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h6)

question: Why is a cup and spoon recommended over a feeding bottle when administering ORS to infants?

options.A: Feeding bottles are harder to clean and can introduce pathogens or cause aspiration
options.B: Bottles completely block the absorption of glucose
options.C: Spoons increase the temperature of the fluid
options.D: Infants cannot swallow liquids from cups at all

explanation: Feeding bottles are notorious for harboring bacteria that cause secondary infections and can increase the risk of aspiration in sick infants. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h6)

question: Which of the following conditions is an absolute contraindication for starting oral rehydration therapy?

options.A: Mild watery diarrhea
options.B: Severe dehydration with hemodynamic shock and impaired consciousness
options.C: Low-grade fever
options.D: Mild nausea without vomiting

explanation: Severe dehydration with shock or impaired consciousness requires immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation rather than oral routes. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h7)

question: What complication can arise if an ORS powder packet is mixed with significantly less water than prescribed?

options.A: Hyponatremia
options.B: Hypernatremia
options.C: Metabolic alkalosis
options.D: Severe hypoglycemia

explanation: Mixing ORS with too little water results in a hypertonic solution, putting the patient at risk for dangerous hypernatremia. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h7)

question: Why is it important to continue feeding and breastfeeding a child during a bout of acute diarrhea?

options.A: It stops diarrhea immediately by slowing gut motility
options.B: It maintains gut integrity, prevents malnutrition, and shortens illness duration
options.C: It replaces the need for oral rehydration salts
options.D: It neutralizes stomach acid

explanation: Continuing appropriate feeding helps preserve intestinal mucosal integrity and prevents the nutritional deficits often worsened by fasting. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h8)

question: What additional micronutrient supplement is commonly recommended alongside ORS by public health authorities to reduce diarrhea severity?

options.A: Iron
options.B: Zinc
options.C: Vitamin C
options.D: Calcium

explanation: Zinc supplementation is clinically proven to reduce the duration and severity of diarrheal episodes and prevent future occurrences. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T18#GNS215_U6_T18_h8)

question: What does the term selective toxicity mean in pharmacology?

options.A: Targeting only gram-negative organisms while completely ignoring gram-positive strains
options.B: Administering multiple drugs simultaneously to reduce overall systemic toxicity
options.C: The ability of a bacterium to survive exposure to a high dose of medication
options.D: Harmful effects restricted only to bacterial target structures without harming host cells

explanation: Selective toxicity ensures that medications damage pathogen physiology while preserving host tissue integrity. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h1)

question: When is empiric antibiotic therapy typically initiated?

options.A: After completing a full course of narrow-spectrum prophylactic medications
options.B: Immediately for acutely ill patients prior to receiving lab culture results
options.C: Only after exact laboratory sensitivities identify the specific causative pathogen
options.D: When a patient develops a severe hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin

explanation: Empiric treatment provides immediate coverage based on clinical presentation while awaiting definitive laboratory data. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h1)

question: Which cellular component is targeted by penicillin and cephalosporin medications?

options.A: 50S ribosomal subunit
options.B: Folic acid pathway
options.C: Peptidoglycan cell wall
options.D: DNA gyrase enzyme

explanation: Beta-lactam drugs weaken the bacterial cell wall by binding to specific proteins, leading to cell lysis. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h2)

question: How do fluoroquinolones exert their antibacterial effect?

options.A: By disrupting bacterial DNA replication through enzyme inhibition
options.B: By acting as a competitive inhibitor in the folic acid synthesis pathway
options.C: By binding directly to the 30S ribosomal subunit to stop translation
options.D: By inserting themselves into the cell membrane to cause ion leakage

explanation: Fluoroquinolones target DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, which are essential for bacterial DNA unwinding and replication. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h2)

question: Why are bactericidal drugs preferred over bacteriostatic drugs in severe infections affecting immunocompromised patients?

options.A: They actively kill the bacteria, requiring less reliance on host immune defenses
options.B: They never cause allergic reactions or adverse gastrointestinal disturbances
options.C: They penetrate the blood-brain barrier much faster than bacteriostatic options
options.D: They can be safely combined with any other class without pharmacological antagonism

explanation: Immunocompromised patients lack sufficient immune response to clear infections, making drugs that directly kill the pathogen essential. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h3)

question: What is the primary action of a bacteriostatic antibacterial drug?

options.A: It stimulates phagocytosis by host neutrophils
options.B: It destroys the peptidoglycan cell wall instantly
options.C: It permanently dissolves bacterial nuclear material
options.D: It inhibits bacterial growth and reproduction

explanation: Bacteriostatic drugs halt replication, depending on the patient's immune system to eliminate the halted bacteria. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h3)

question: What is a primary clinical advantage of using a narrow-spectrum antibiotic over a broad-spectrum one?

options.A: It prevents the development of renal toxicity in elderly populations
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for prior laboratory culture and sensitivity tests
options.C: It preserves normal patient microflora and decreases superinfection risks
options.D: It works faster against multiple polymicrobial infections simultaneously

explanation: Narrow-spectrum drugs target specific pathogens, leaving beneficial commensal bacteria largely unharmed. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h4)

question: Which condition is a frequent complication associated with broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy due to the disruption of normal flora?

options.A: Clostridioides difficile colitis
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Essential hypertension
options.D: Type 2 diabetes mellitus

explanation: Killing normal intestinal flora with broad-spectrum drugs allows resistant organisms like Clostridioides difficile to proliferate. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h4)

question: How do beta-lactamase enzymes protect bacteria from penicillin-class drugs?

options.A: By altering the outer membrane porins to block drug entry completely
options.B: By chemically breaking down the antibiotic molecule before it reaches its target
options.C: By thickening the peptidoglycan wall to prevent drug penetration
options.D: By pumping the drug out of the cell cytoplasm via active transport channels

explanation: Beta-lactamases hydrolyze the beta-lactam ring, rendering the antibiotic inactive. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of antimicrobial stewardship programs in healthcare facilities?

options.A: To completely replace broad-spectrum drugs with herbal alternatives
options.B: To optimize treatment outcomes and minimize the emergence of resistant strains
options.C: To reduce hospital admission rates for patients with chronic viral infections
options.D: To lower the financial cost of laboratory culture and sensitivity testing

explanation: Stewardship ensures appropriate drug selection and duration to cure infections while preventing resistance. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h5)

question: Which two major organ systems are most commonly monitored for toxicity when administering aminoglycoside antibiotics?

options.A: Kidneys and ears
options.B: Heart and lungs
options.C: Skin and liver
options.D: Brain and spleen

explanation: Aminoglycosides carry a high risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, necessitating close monitoring. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h6)

question: A patient receiving intravenous penicillin develops sudden laryngeal edema, wheezing, and hives. What type of reaction is occurring?

options.A: A normal secondary superinfection response
options.B: Type IV delayed cell-mediated hypersensitivity
options.C: Type I immediate IgE-mediated hypersensitivity
options.D: Direct systemic organ-specific nephrotoxicity

explanation: Anaphylaxis and acute hives following beta-lactam exposure are classic IgE-mediated allergic reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h6)

question: Why is it vital to collect laboratory culture specimens BEFORE starting the first dose of an antibacterial drug?

options.A: Cultures take several days to grow, and treatment should never be delayed for labs
options.B: Baseline blood urea nitrogen levels will be altered if cultures are drawn too late
options.C: The laboratory requires antibiotic residue in the sample to identify the organism
options.D: Starting antibiotics beforehand can suppress the pathogen and yield false-negative cultures

explanation: Administering antibiotics first can kill or suppress the bacteria in the sample, leading to missed diagnoses. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h7)

question: What is a primary nursing instruction when educating a patient prescribed a 10-day course of oral antibiotics?

options.A: Double the next scheduled dose if a single daily administration time is missed
options.B: Complete the entire course of medication even if symptoms disappear after three days
options.C: Store all unfinished tablets in the home medicine cabinet for future infections
options.D: Stop taking the capsules immediately once the fever subsides to prevent liver strain

explanation: Patients must finish the full course to eradicate all bacteria and prevent resistant strain selection. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T2#GNS215_U6_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary reason antifungal drugs often produce more adverse effects than antibacterial agents?

options.A: Fungi are eukaryotic and share cellular similarities with human hosts
options.B: Fungal cell walls are composed of thick peptidoglycan layers
options.C: Fungi multiply at a significantly faster rate than bacteria
options.D: Antifungal medications are exclusively administered through the intravenous route

explanation: Because fungi are eukaryotic like human cells, finding targets that harm the fungus without damaging host tissue is biochemically difficult, reducing selective toxicity. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h1)

question: Which environmental factor heavily contributes to the high prevalence of superficial fungal infections in tropical regions such as Nigeria?

options.A: Widespread soil acidification
options.B: Low barometric pressure
options.C: High ambient humidity and heat
options.D: Frequent exposure to cold winds

explanation: Dermatophytes and yeasts thrive in warm, moist environments, making tropical climates exceptionally favorable for superficial fungal proliferation. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h1)

question: Which class of antifungal medications acts by inhibiting the synthesis of beta-1,3-D-glucan in the fungal cell wall?

options.A: Polyenes
options.B: Azoles
options.C: Echinocandins
options.D: Allylamines

explanation: Echinocandins target the fungal cell wall by blocking beta-1,3-D-glucan synthesis, causing osmotic instability and cell lysis. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h2)

question: How do azole antifungal agents primarily disrupt fungal cellular integrity?

options.A: By blocking lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase to prevent ergosterol production
options.B: By entering the fungal nucleus and permanently alkylating DNA strands
options.C: By degrading chitin fibers located within the outer capsule
options.D: By physically binding directly to existing ergosterol molecules to form pores

explanation: Azoles inhibit the fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme responsible for synthesizing ergosterol, leading to defective, leaky cell membranes. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h2)

question: What is the primary dose-limiting toxicity associated with conventional Amphotericin B administration?

options.A: Ototoxicity
options.B: Hepatotoxicity
options.C: Nephrotoxicity
options.D: Cardiotoxicity

explanation: Amphotericin B causes vasoconstriction of renal blood vessels and direct tubular injury, making kidney damage its most concerning side effect. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h3)

question: A patient with a confirmed Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis infection requires a systemic antifungal drug known for excellent penetration into the cerebrospinal fluid. Which medication is most appropriate?

options.A: Fluconazole
options.B: Nystatin
options.C: Caspofungin
options.D: Terbinafine

explanation: Fluconazole has unique pharmacokinetic properties that allow it to cross the blood-brain barrier effectively, making it ideal for central nervous system fungal infections. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h3)

question: Which cellular enzyme is specifically inhibited by allylamine antifungals like terbinafine?

options.A: Lanosterol demethylase
options.B: Squalene epoxidase
options.C: Beta-1,3-glucan synthase
options.D: DNA polymerase

explanation: Allylamines block squalene epoxidase, preventing the conversion of squalene to ergosterol and causing intracellular toxicity from squalene buildup. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h4)

question: Why is nystatin administered as an oral suspension for local thrush rather than an intravenous injection?

options.A: It is poorly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract into the bloodstream
options.B: It is rapidly destroyed by gastric acid before reaching the stomach
options.C: It is extremely toxic to the liver when given parenterally
options.D: It precipitates immediately when mixed with human blood plasma

explanation: Nystatin's systemic toxicity is too high for safe injection, but its poor GI absorption makes it safe and effective for topical treatment of mucosal surfaces. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h4)

question: How do systemic azole antifungals typically alter the plasma concentrations of concurrently administered drugs like warfarin?

options.A: They displace the drugs from renal tubules, increasing urinary excretion speed
options.B: They induce liver enzymes, causing faster elimination and lower drug levels
options.C: On the contrary, they inhibit hepatic enzymes, raising drug levels and toxicity risk
options.D: They bind directly to the drugs in the stomach, preventing all absorption

explanation: Azoles inhibit hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, slowing down the metabolism of companion drugs and leading to toxic accumulation in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h5)

question: A patient scheduled for an intravenous infusion of Amphotericin B is at high risk for acute infusion-related rigors and fever. What preventive measure should the nurse anticipate?

options.A: Refrigerating the intravenous bag to near-freezing temperatures
options.B: Administering a prophylactic dose of a rapid-acting loop diuretic
options.C: Diluting the medication in 500 mL of 0.9% normal saline exclusively
options.D: Pre-medicating with antipyretics, antihistamines, or hydrocortisone

explanation: Infusion reactions caused by cytokine release from amphotericin B are commonly managed with prophylactic anti-inflammatory and antipyretic medications. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h5)

question: What is a critical electrolyte disturbance commonly associated with intravenous polyene therapy that requires active nursing surveillance?

options.A: Hypoglycemia and hyperkalemia
options.B: Hyponatremia and hyperchloremia
options.C: Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia
options.D: Hypercalcemia and hyperphosphatemia

explanation: Polyenes alter distal renal tubule permeability, causing renal wasting of potassium and magnesium, which necessitates frequent electrolyte monitoring. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h6)

question: What instruction is essential when educating a patient who has been prescribed a topical antifungal cream for a skin dermatophyte infection?

options.A: Wash the skin with harsh antiseptic soap immediately before every application
options.B: Stop applying the cream the exact day the visible rash completely disappears
options.C: Apply a thick, occlusive plastic bandage over the cream to speed up absorption
options.D: Continue applying the medication for a week after lesions clear to prevent relapse

explanation: Fungal spores often persist on the skin even after visual signs of infection vanish; continuing treatment prevents early recurrence. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T3#GNS215_U6_T3_h6)

question: What anatomical barrier significantly limits systemic drug penetration into the anterior segment of the eye?

options.A: The lens capsule and vitreous humor
options.B: The cornea and blood-aqueous barrier
options.C: The retina and Bruch's membrane
options.D: The sclera and choroid plexus

explanation: The cornea and blood-aqueous barrier protect intraocular structures and restrict the entry of systemically administered drugs, making topical administration necessary for anterior segment conditions. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T4#GNS215_U6_T4_h1)

question: Why must otic drops containing aminoglycosides be avoided when the tympanic membrane is ruptured?

options.A: They can enter the middle ear and cause permanent sensorineural hearing loss
options.B: They will immediately crystallize and block the external auditory canal
options.C: They neutralize normal flora and worsen bacterial resistance instantly
options.D: They cause severe systemic hypertension through rapid mucosal absorption

explanation: A compromised tympanic membrane allows otic drops to cross into the middle and inner ear, where ototoxic drugs can damage cochlear hair cells and lead to permanent deafness. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T4#GNS215_U6_T4_h1)

question: Which class of glaucoma medication primarily increases uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor?

options.A: Beta-adrenergic blockers
options.B: Prostaglandin analogues
options.C: Osmotic diuretics
options.D: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

explanation: Prostaglandin analogues like latanoprost reduce intraocular pressure by enhancing the uveoscleral outflow pathway and are dosed once daily. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T4#GNS215_U6_T4_h2)

question: A patient with a history of bronchial asthma is prescribed timolol eye drops for glaucoma. What is the most significant clinical concern with this prescription?

options.A: Topical timolol inactivates inhaled asthma medications instantly
options.B: It will cause irreversible widening of the pupil diameter
options.C: The drug will completely stop aqueous humor production permanently
options.D: Systemic absorption can trigger severe bronchospasm

explanation: Even though administered topically, beta-blockers like timolol can enter the systemic circulation and provoke bronchoconstriction in patients with reactive airway diseases. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T4#GNS215_U6_T4_h2)

question: What is the primary pharmacological effect of a cycloplegic eye drop?

options.A: Contraction of the pupillary sphincter muscle and miosis
options.B: Suppression of bacterial growth in the conjunctival sac
options.C: Paralysis of the ciliary muscle and loss of accommodation
options.D: Increased systemic blood pressure via alpha-receptor agonism

explanation: Cycloplegics block acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors on the ciliary body, paralyzing the focusing mechanism and causing mydriasis. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T4#GNS215_U6_T4_h3)

question: Why are short-acting cycloplegics preferred over long-acting agents like atropine for routine diagnostic refraction in adults?

options.A: They do not cause any degree of papillary dilation
options.B: They lower intraocular pressure much faster than atropine
options.C: They completely eliminate the risk of systemic absorption
options.D: They prevent prolonged blurring of vision and photophobia

explanation: Long-acting agents like atropine can blur near vision and cause light sensitivity for over a week, whereas agents like tropicamide wear off in hours. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T4#GNS215_U6_T4_h3)

question: Which of the following is a recognized long-term complication of prolonged topical corticosteroid eye drop use?

options.A: Spontaneous rupture of the corneal stroma
